snip.t: Keep the alternatives open: a mood disorder with psychotic features (mania or depression), substance-induced psychosis (cannabis, khat, alcohol), and a medical or neurological cause (HIV, epilepsy, head injury, thyroid, delirium).
Psychomotor agitation or retardation; overactivity and disinhibition (mania).
Pressured speech (mania); poverty of speech and mutism (depression, schizophrenia); slow, monotonous (depression); dysarthria or slurring (neurological, intoxication).
Mania: Sustained period of abnormally elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy and goal-directed activity.
Flight of ideas: Rapid flow of accelerated speech with abrupt changes from topic to topic, but with recognizable links; typical of mania.
The classic mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder (prevention and mania).

Psychiatric emergencies: Suicidal behaviour, violence, acute psychosis and mania, severe depression, delirium, substance-related emergencies, agitation, catatonia, special populations and other crises

faq.a: Severe malaria can lead to cerebral malaria, which presents with delirium rather than classic mania; however, malaria‑associated neuropsychiatric symptoms can mimic mania in endemic areas.
Khat can induce a manic‑like state; cessation often leads to symptom resolution, but chronic use may precipitate bipolar disorder.
Avoid lithium; use valproate with caution (monitor liver enzymes) or consider carbamazepine; always weigh risks versus benefits.
faq.q: What if the patient is pregnant?

exam: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected mania in a low‑resource setting? — Assess safety, rule out medical causes, and start a mood stabiliser.
How would you differentiate mania from delirium at the bedside? — Mania: alert, pressured speech, grandiosity; delirium: fluctuating consciousness, inattention.
A patient with mania is also on antiretroviral therapy. What drug interaction should you monitor? — Valproate can increase levels of efavirenz; monitor for neurotoxicity.
Which laboratory test is most critical to rule out before starting a mood stabiliser? — Thyroid function tests to exclude hyperthyroidism.
A patient presents with rapid mood swings and recent khat use. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Substance‑induced mania; treat by stopping khat and providing supportive care.
What is the preferred antipsychotic for acute agitation in a patient with a history of hepatitis B? — Haloperidol (low hepatic metabolism) rather than olanzapine.
Why is lithium avoided in patients with renal impairment? — It is excreted renally and can cause nephrotoxicity.
ai.title: Mania
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Mania is a sustained, abnormally elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and goal‑directed activity. It requires rapid assessment for safety, ruling out medical causes, and initiation of mood stabilisation.

b: Mood must be markedly different from patient’s baseline; symptoms must cause marked impairment or require hospitalization.
sections.p: Mania is defined by DSM‑5 as a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood lasting at least one week (or less if hospitalization is required). The episode is accompanied by at least three of the following: inflated self‑esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal‑directed activity, or excessive involvement in risky behaviours.

b: Severe mania (YMRS >30) often needs inpatient care and antipsychotic cover.
sections.p: The Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) is the most common tool; a score >20 indicates moderate to severe mania. In low‑resource settings, a simple bedside score (e.g., 3–5 items) can guide urgency.

b: Khat chewing is common and can trigger or worsen mania.
sections.p: Primary cause is bipolar disorder. In East Africa, consider substance‑induced (khat, alcohol, cannabis), infections (HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B), thyroid dysfunction, and metabolic disturbances. Herbal remedies may also precipitate mania.

b: Look for pressured speech, flight of ideas, and decreased sleep.
sections.p: Patients appear restless, talk rapidly, have grandiose ideas, and may engage in impulsive spending or risky sexual behaviour. They may also exhibit psychomotor agitation, distractibility, and impaired judgment.

If a test is unavailable, rely on clinical history and basic bedside signs; for example, a rapid assessment of thyroid function can be approximated by looking for tremor, weight loss, and heat intolerance.

t.b: Rule out anaemia or infection; anaemia can mimic or worsen mania.
Hypo‑ or hyperthyroidism can present with mania; a low TSH with high free T4 suggests hyperthyroidism.
HIV infection is common and can present with neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Hepatitis B/C can cause hepatic encephalopathy or mood changes.
Hyponatraemia or hypokalaemia can precipitate delirium or affect mood.
Detects recent khat, cannabis, or alcohol use.

b: Any sign of self‑harm or aggression warrants immediate safety assessment.
sections.p: Urgent red flags include suicidal ideation, homicidal thoughts, severe agitation leading to violence, or rapid deterioration in cognition. Complications may be metabolic (e.g., hyperglycaemia), cardiovascular (tachyarrhythmias), or infectious (sepsis from self‑injury).

b: Valproate is preferred in pregnancy; carbamazepine is effective but monitor liver enzymes.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Initiate a mood stabiliser (e.g., sodium valproate or carbamazepine) and consider a low‑dose antipsychotic (e.g., haloperidol) for acute agitation. Benzodiazepines can be used for severe agitation but avoid long‑term use.

b: Regular review of mood symptoms and medication side‑effects is essential.
sections.p: After acute control, arrange outpatient follow‑up with a psychiatrist or primary care provider. Educate the patient and family about medication adherence, substance avoidance, and early warning signs.

b: Delirium shows fluctuating consciousness; mania maintains alertness.
sections.p: Differential includes delirium, acute psychosis, substance‑induced psychosis, and severe depression with psychotic features.

b: Always repeat tests if clinical suspicion remains high.
sections.p: A normal thyroid panel does not exclude central hypothyroidism; a negative HIV test may be false early in infection. Low sodium can be masked by dehydration.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of metabolic or infectious complications
